node-1.label: Patient has rising PSA levels despite androgen deprivation therapy

node-2.label: Patient is a 70-year-old male with a history of primary radiotherapy for prostate cancer

node-3.label: PSA level is 6 ng/mL and PSA doubling time is 6.6 months

node-5.label: Patient was evaluated at a tertiary referral institution; no specific physical examination findings were detailed in the report

why.why: Both the laboratory physician and radiologist analyses independently confirm that confirmed castrate testosterone and three consecutive PSA rises with two 50% increases over nadir and PSA >2 ng/mL meet CRPC progression criteria despite ADT. The radiologist adds that the absence of contemporaneous imaging does not weaken the CRPC diagnosis itself. These expert validations support the earlier evidence of rising PSA with a short doubling time, raising confidence from 0.88 to 0.90.

Confirmed castrate testosterone levels directly rule out inadequate androgen suppression as the cause of rising PSA. Since there is no testosterone deficiency or evidence of noncompliance, the previous lower-confidence alternative is no longer viable; confidence is reduced from 0.18 to 0.02.

Neuroendocrine transformation remains unlikely because the PSA pattern is atypical and there is no biopsy confirmation of neuroendocrine differentiation. The expert analysis reiterates these limitations despite the prior radiotherapy history, so confidence is reduced from 0.10 to 0.05.

node-9.label: Testosterone level is confirmed to be in castrate range

node-10.label: PSA shows three consecutive rises with two 50% increases over nadir and PSA >2 ng/mL

node-12.label: There is no biopsy confirmation of neuroendocrine transformation

why.why: Both the radiologist and laboratory physician reaffirm biochemical M0 CRPC as the leading subtype, based on negative pre-operative imaging, castrate testosterone, good performance status, and the typical PSA pattern. However, both also highlight that no contemporaneous imaging is available at PSA progression, and the radiologist specifically recommends PSMA PET/CT for definitive staging; therefore M0 remains probable but not directly confirmed. Confidence is maintained at 0.78 rather than increased.

CRPC progression is established, and both experts state that occult M1 cannot be fully excluded without contemporaneous imaging. The radiologist’s recommendation for PSMA PET/CT and the laboratory physician’s call for supplementary bone scan/CT acknowledge this residual uncertainty, so M1 remains a non-negligible lower-probability subtype; confidence remains 0.15.

attrs.why: This is a rare subtype of CRPC progression. The atypical PSA pattern and lack of biopsy confirmation of neuroendocrine differentiation (node-12) argue against it, but prior radiotherapy (node-2) and rising PSA despite castrate testosterone keep it as a low-probability refinement worth considering.
